overview: A three-week introduction for people with no technical background. Learners find out what AI is, how machines learn patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules, and where AI already shapes the products they use every day. There is no maths and no code. Every idea is taught through everyday analogies and a free, browser-based tool. By the end, learners train their own image classifier and can judge, with a simple checklist, when to trust an AI system and when to question it.

time_plan.per_week: About 20 minutes of video, 60 minutes of exercises and quizzes, and 40 minutes of reading and reflection. In week 3 that last block goes to the capstone.

objectives.text: Define artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI, and describe how they relate to each other.
Explain in plain language how a model learns from labelled examples, using the terms data, features, labels, training and prediction.
Compare supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning using everyday examples.
Train and test a simple image classifier in Google Teachable Machine.
Identify AI features in everyday products and infer what data each one probably learns from.
Judge how reliable an AI output or use case is by considering test results, overfitting, bias and hallucination.
Write a one-page explanation of how a self-trained classifier learned, where it fails, and why.

modules.title: What AI Is and Where You Meet It

lessons.title: What Is AI, Really?
lessons.summary: AI as systems that perform tasks we link with human intelligence. The difference between following rules and learning from examples. AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI shown as nested circles.
lessons.exercise: Sort 8 everyday systems into 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from examples', then compare with the answer key.

lessons.title: AI in Your Day
lessons.summary: A day-in-the-life tour: spam filters, video and music recommendations, map travel times, phone face unlock, translation and voice assistants. For each one: what it predicts, and what data it probably learned from.
lessons.exercise: Keep an 'AI diary' for one day: list 5 AI features you used and guess what each one predicts.

lessons.title: Learning from Examples: Data, Features and Labels
lessons.summary: Analogy: a child learning to tell cats from dogs by seeing many labelled pictures. Data, features and labels. Why the quantity, variety and quality of examples matter.
lessons.exercise: Choose features and labels for a fruit-sorting machine, then list 3 examples that could confuse it.

lessons.title: Training vs. Using a Model
lessons.summary: The two phases: training (finding patterns) and prediction, also called inference (applying them to new examples). Analogy: studying for an exam vs. sitting the exam. Models do not 'look up' answers.
lessons.exercise: Ask a free AI chatbot (ChatGPT or Claude) to explain training vs. inference to a 10-year-old, then mark one thing it got right and one thing it simplified.

lessons.title: Supervised Learning: Classification and Regression
lessons.summary: Learning with an answer key. Classification predicts a category (spam or not spam). Regression predicts a number (a delivery time). Worked examples from several countries and industries.
lessons.exercise: Label 10 business questions as classification or regression.

lessons.title: Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning
lessons.summary: Unsupervised learning finds groups without labels (customer segments). Reinforcement learning learns from rewards through trial and error (game-playing agents). When to use each of the three types.
lessons.exercise: Match 6 scenarios to supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning, and justify one choice in a sentence.

lessons.title: Neural Networks Without the Maths
lessons.summary: A neural network as layers of adjustable 'dials' (weights). Learning means nudging the dials to reduce mistakes, repeated many times. Why 'deep' means many layers. No equations.
lessons.exercise: Guess-and-adjust game: tune two sliders on a worksheet to hit a target, then write down how this resembles training.

lessons.title: Testing a Model: Accuracy and Overfitting
lessons.summary: Why a model is tested on examples it never saw. What accuracy means and what it hides. Overfitting explained as a student who memorised the practice exam.
lessons.exercise: Read two short model 'report cards' and decide which model you would trust, and why.

modules.title: What AI Can and Cannot Do

lessons.title: Generative AI and Chatbots
lessons.summary: Large language models learn to predict the next piece of text. That explains both their fluency and their confident mistakes (hallucinations). What 'generating' means for images too, at a high level.
lessons.exercise: Ask a chatbot 3 factual questions you can check, verify each answer, and record any errors.

lessons.title: Bias, Data and the Limits of AI
lessons.summary: Biased or unrepresentative data leads to unfair outputs. Other limits: privacy, lack of real-world understanding, and changing conditions. Illustrated with hypothetical cases rather than named incidents.
lessons.exercise: For a hypothetical hiring or loan model, list 3 ways the training data could be unrepresentative.

lessons.title: Build Your Own Image Classifier
lessons.summary: A walkthrough of Google Teachable Machine: create 2–3 classes, capture example images, train, then test with new images. Connects each step back to data, labels, training and testing. [VERSION] Interface steps may change.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 1: train a classifier with at least 2 classes and 20+ images per class, then test it on 10 new images and record the results.

lessons.title: Should I Trust This AI? A Practical Checklist
lessons.summary: A 5-question checklist: What data did it learn from? How was it tested? Who could it fail? Can I verify the output? What happens if it is wrong? Then the capstone brief and rubric.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 2: write a one-page explanation of how your classifier learned, where it failed, and why.

capstone.title: Train and Explain an Image Classifier
capstone.brief: Train a simple image classifier with Google Teachable Machine and write a one-page explanation of how it learned.
